name: Cheapest-per-GB VRAM is not value: two join artifacts produced a 60x and an 80x false ranking, and the real answer is that only six accelerators in this corpus can be ranked at all
symptom: Asked for the cheapest configuration that can genuinely serve VRAM, the corpus produced a table where a $310 supply record paired with a 96GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and came out as the best value in the database at 5636 tok/s per $1000, and where the RTX 4090 came out as the worst at 456621 tok/s per $1000 - roughly 80x below the RTX 5090, the opposite of every measurement the corpus actually holds. Both figures come from real records. Both are artefacts of the join, not of the hardware.
root_cause:
Two records attach a number to an accelerator the number does not describe.

ARTEFACT 1 - PRICE OVER-ATTRIBUTION. data/supply/microcenter-in-store-gpus.json carried accelerator_ids ['intel-arc-b580', 'intel-arc-pro-b60', 'nvidia-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell'] against a single price of 309.99. The price_basis names exactly one item: an ASRock Intel Arc B580 Challenger OC 12GB bare card. The other two ids are parts that appeared on the same listing page. A join that pairs price x benchmark therefore divided a 12GB card's price by a 600W 96GB workstation card's throughput (55 tok/s on Llama 3.3 70B Q8_0) and reported the RTX PRO 6000 as 60x better value than it is.

ARTEFACT 2 - THROUGHPUT UNDER-ATTRIBUTION. data/benchmarks/comm-4090-llamacpp-rpc-3-host-decode-tok-s.json held 4.38 tok/s with accelerator_ids ['nvidia-rtx-4090']. That figure is a THREE-HOST llama.cpp RPC cluster totalling 56GB - one RTX 4090 plus two RTX 4060 Ti - on the reporter's first attempt, single request, n_ctx_slot 8192. It is not a per-card 4090 figure. Filed under the 4090's id it became the 4090's only decode benchmark and dragged the card to the bottom of the ranking.
workaround:
Both records were corrected on 2026-10-11 and the ranking recomputed. The join rules that follow from them are the real deliverable:

RULE A - a supply record's price attaches to the item its price_basis NAMES, not to every accelerator the page mentions. A listing page covering several parts needs either one accelerator_id plus a basis that names that part, or per-part prices.

RULE B - a per-card tok/s is the denominator of every value figure in this corpus. A cluster, RPC, or multi-host figure must not be filed under one card's accelerator_ids. Where no record type fits a mixed configuration, leave the list empty and name the machines in the methodology text.

With both artefacts removed, the honest local tok/s-per-dollar table (cheapest capex source per card, batch size 1 in every row, from records in this corpus):

  tok/s per $1000  accelerator                 capex     tok/s  model (VRAM)
  14279            nvidia-rtx-5090            $  1999   140.00 Qwen3-14B-AWQ (32GB)
  23518            nvidia-rtx-5090            $  1999    85.00 Qwen3 32B Q4_K_M (32GB)
  29867            amd-radeon-rx-7900-xtx     $  1406    47.06 Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_XL (24GB)
  44422            nvidia-rtx-5090            $  1999    45.00 Llama 3.3 70B Q4_K_M (32GB)
  100769           nvidia-rtx-5080            $  6550    65.00 Qwen3 32B Q4_K_M (16GB)
  302254           nvidia-rtx-pro-6000-bl     $ 16624    55.00 Llama 3.3 70B Q8_0 (96GB)

Read the ordering carefully - it is dominated by which model each card was measured on, not by the cards. The RTX PRO 6000's low tok/s-per-$1000 comes from running a 70B at Q8_0 at 55 tok/s on a $16.6k card, not from being slow. Cross-model comparisons within this table are not value findings.

THE HONEST LIMIT: these SIX are the only accelerators in the entire corpus that have both a non-cloud price and a decode benchmark. Sixteen priced accelerators have no decode benchmark at all and are therefore unknowns, not picks. The ones a buyer would most want to rank are in that list: RTX 3090 ($1100, 24GB), RTX 4090 ($2000, 24GB), RX 9070 XT ($829, 16GB), Arc B580 ($200-330, 12GB), A100 80GB PCIe ($12109, 80GB), A100 80GB SXM4 ($2499, 80GB), RTX 5070 Ti ($6550, 16GB), RTX 4080 ($16624, 16GB), H100 PCIe ($43000, 80GB). The corpus cannot say which of them is good value, only which has been measured.
notes:
FILED 2026-10-11 (parent, in place of a subagent that died on HTTP 429 before making a tool call). The question asked was what the cheapest genuinely-usable VRAM configuration is, comparing 2x Tesla M40 (48GB) against 1x P40 (24GB) against a single 4090 (32GB). That comparison cannot be answered from this corpus, and the reason is itself the finding: the M40 and P40 have supply records and no decode benchmark of any kind, so the corpus holds their price and nothing about what they run. Tesla M40 24GB at $189 is $7.88/GB and is the cheapest VRAM in the database; it is also tensor-coreless Maxwell with compute capability 5.2, so it cannot run fast decode, and the corpus has no tok/s number that would let a reader see that for themselves.

The one thing the corpus CAN say from real paired records: on Strix Halo (gfx1151, 128GB LPDDR5X, 256 GB/s bus), dense Qwen2.5-72B Q5_K_M runs at 4.1 tok/s while GPT-OSS 120B MXFP4 MoE reaches 49.0 tok/s on the same machine - see llamacpp-strix-halo-8060s-qwen2-5-72b-q5-k-m-decode and llamacpp-strix-halo-8060s-gpt-oss-120b-mxfp4-decode. A 12x difference decided entirely by whether the model is dense, because only active experts are streamed. That is the strongest value-shaped result the corpus holds, and it is about model choice rather than hardware choice.

PICKS BY MODEL SIZE, as the value brief asked. Same corpus records, split by
which model class the card has actually been measured on, because a card's
rank depends entirely on which row you read:

SMALL/MEDIUM MODELS (14-32B) - the 5090 is the only card with a real
small-model figure, and it is a strong one:
  nvidia-rtx-5090        $1,999   140.00 tok/s  Qwen3-14B-AWQ (awq_marlin)  batch 1  = 14279 tok/s per $1000
  nvidia-rtx-5090        $1,999    85.00 tok/s  Qwen3 32B Q4_K_M          batch 1  = 23518 tok/s per $1000
  amd-radeon-rx-7900-xtx $1,406    47.06 tok/s  Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_XL       batch 1  = 29867 tok/s per $1000
The 7900 XTX is the best value in this class on a pure ratio, and it is the
only AMD card in the corpus with a decode benchmark on a mid-size model.

LARGE MODELS (70B):
  nvidia-rtx-5090        $1,999    45.00 tok/s  Llama 3.3 70B Q4_K_M      batch 1  = 44422 tok/s per $1000
  nvidia-rtx-pro-6000-bl $16,624    55.00 tok/s  Llama 3.3 70B Q8_0       batch 1  = 302254 tok/s per $1000
The 5090 runs 70B Q4_K_M at 45 tok/s on 32GB. The RTX PRO 6000 runs 70B at
Q8_0 - a materially higher-quality quant - on 96GB, and its poor ratio is a
consequence of paying $16.6k for headroom and precision, not of being slow.
These two are not competing for the same buyer.

VRAM GATES, which decide the class before any ratio does:
  nvidia-rtx-5090              32GB  - fits 70B Q4_K_M, not 70B at Q8
  amd-radeon-rx-7900-xtx       24GB  - fits 27B Q4_K_XL (17.5GB), not 70B
  nvidia-rtx-5080              16GB  - 32B Q4 only, no 70B row exists
  intel-arc-b580               12GB  - fits 8-14B only
  amd-radeon-rx-9070-xt        16GB  - fits 32B Q4
A card that cannot fit the model is not a candidate at any price, so the VRAM
gate is applied before the tok/s-per-dollar split rather than after. | PRICE-ATTRIBUTION CORRECTION 2026-10-11 (crawler/w17-dc-capex): the RTX 4080 capex ($16,624) and the RTX 5070 Ti capex ($6,550) quoted in this gotcha were NOT prices for those cards. Both were over-attributions from supply records whose price_basis names a different part (the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and the RTX 5090 respectively). The offending accelerator_ids have been removed from bh-photo-used-workstation-gpus, bh-photo-workstation-gpus and new-retail-rtx-5090-amazon. After the fix NEITHER the RTX 4080 NOR the RTX 5070 Ti has any non-cloud price_usd in the corpus, so neither can be ranked on value at all.
